findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Ensure the forced-`nt` tests cannot drive the real Windows walk with a fake pid, either via an injectable snapshot/terminate seam or a guard, and state how this holds on the Windows sweep.
evidence: "The 2 forced-`nt` tests ... keep passing unchanged because kill+wait stay and the walk failure is caught."
"any failure (no `kernel32` on a forced-`nt` POSIX test host, access denied) is logged at debug"
findings.finding: The 2 forced-`nt` tests in test_acli_subprocess_timeout.py are said to pass unchanged because 'the walk failure is caught'. That reasoning holds only on a POSIX host. On the Windows sweep, kernel32 exists, so the real CreateToolhelp32Snapshot/TerminateProcess walk runs against _FakeProc's fabricated pid. It could terminate any real process whose (possibly stale) parent pid equals that number.
scenarios: The Windows sweep runs test_acli_subprocess_timeout. _FakeProc.pid matches a stale parent pid on the runner, and the walk kills a runner process, producing a flaky or broken CI job.
findings.suggested_fix: Route the walk through module-level snapshot/terminate callables, which test_proc_reap_windows.py already fakes. Either have the forced-nt tests patch them to no-ops, or skip the walk when `proc` is not a real subprocess.Popen. If this requires editing test_acli_subprocess_timeout.py, drop 'must pass unchanged' from Scope.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State how test_harness treats a zombie grandchild on POSIX (e.g. _pid_alive or a /proc state check counts zombies as dead), so the 10 s poll does not depend on init reaping.

findings.finding: The test_harness rewrite polls (10 s) until the killed grandchild is dead on POSIX, and relies on init reaping the orphan zombie. Under a PID 1 that does not reap (e.g. a container without an init), the zombie persists. Whether _pid_alive then reads it as alive is not stated, so the test may time out regardless of the fix.
scenarios: make verify runs inside a dev container whose PID 1 does not reap, and test_harness fails after 10 s even though the reap worked.

findings.finding: The plan assumes tests/unit/store/test_git_locking_no_fcntl.py only needs its patch target changed ('patches lock_kernel.fcntl/msvcrt instead'). findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In the test_harness grandchild check, count a POSIX zombie as dead (e.g. read the process state from /proc/<pid>/stat, or `ps -o stat=`, and accept 'Z'), and keep _pid_alive's OpenProcess/WaitForSingleObject probe only for the Windows branch.
evidence: Plan: "polled (bounded, 10 s) until dead after the timeout on every platform, since on POSIX a killed orphan stays a zombie until init reaps it (liveness via `lock_owner._pid_alive`...)"
src/rebar/_store/lock_owner.py:309-330: on POSIX _pid_alive returns True unless os.kill(pid, 0) raises ProcessLookupError, which never happens for a zombie

src/rebar/grounding/harness.py:174-175: start_new_session puts the grandchild in the child's group, so killpg kills it, but the grandchild is the CHILD's child and is reparented to init/subreaper, not to the test process
findings.finding: The test_harness change polls lock_owner._pid_alive until the grandchild is 'dead'. On POSIX _pid_alive is os.kill(pid, 0), which succeeds for a zombie, so a killed orphan still reads as alive. The plan itself says the killed orphan 'stays a zombie until init reaps it', so the 10 s poll only passes if some reaper collects the orphan in time. Under a non-reaping PID 1 (e.g. a container where the test runner or a plain shell is PID 1) the zombie never goes away, and the test fails even though the reaper did kill the grandchild.
findings.location: Approach (this change) — Tests bullet (test_harness grandchild liveness poll)
scenarios: make verify or CI run inside a container without --init: PID 1 never calls waitpid, the grandchild stays a zombie, _pid_alive keeps returning True, and the test fails after 10 s.
A slow-reaping init on a loaded runner makes the test flaky.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test-local helper `_gone(pid)`. On Windows, return `not lock_owner._pid_alive(pid)`. On POSIX, return True if os.kill(pid, 0) raises ProcessLookupError or the process state (from /proc/<pid>/stat on Linux, `ps -o stat= -p <pid>` elsewhere) starts with 'Z'. Poll that helper within the 10 s bound.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In the `_proc.reap_process_group` Approach bullet, compare the snapshot walk with Job Objects (KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE / TerminateJobObject at spawn time) and with psutil `children(recursive=True)`, and record why the walk was chosen (for example: keeping the stdlib-only leaf, not changing the five Popen call sites, CI already running in a job) or switch to a job object.
evidence: Plan: "a `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot` walk (ctypes, Windows only) collects processes whose parent-pid chain leads to `proc.pid`, and each gets `TerminateProcess`; a second pass catches any started meanwhile."
Absence: the plan never mentions Job Objects, TerminateJobObject, KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE or psutil, and gives no reason for choosing a snapshot walk over them.

Zed fixed the same orphaned-grandchild bug this way: "Assign spawned processes to a job object with JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE so the whole tree is terminated on kill" (zed-industries/zed PR #58885). Cargo's job.rs and a GitLab Runner proposal use the same approach.

Microsoft Job Objects docs: child processes created by a process in a job are associated with the job by default, and KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE terminates all associated processes when the last handle closes.

Repo: five sites spawn the Popen and pass it to reap_process_group (src/rebar/_bridge_runner.py:156, grounding/harness.py:121, _store/gitutil.py:311, reconciler/adapters/jira/acli_subprocess.py:476, jira_family/wiki_render.py:397), so a job-object design would mean changing those spawn sites. That trade-off should be stated.
findings.finding: The Windows descendant-kill design is a hand-written ctypes CreateToolhelp32Snapshot/TerminateProcess walk over parent pids. The plan does not consider Job Objects, the standard Windows way to tear down a process tree. Assigning the child to a job with JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE (or calling TerminateJobObject) kills every descendant, including orphaned grandchildren, with no pid walk, no second pass for processes started meanwhile, and no PID-reuse risk. Mature projects use it for exactly this bug. The plan also does not mention psutil's `children(recursive=True)` as the existing version of the walk it is rebuilding.
scenarios: A grandchild spawns a great-grandchild between the two snapshot passes, and that process escapes. A job would hold it automatically.
A reviewer or maintainer cannot tell whether the bespoke walk was chosen deliberately or because job objects were overlooked.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short 'Alternatives considered' paragraph to the `_proc` bullet. Either (a) adopt a job object: create it via ctypes, assign `proc._handle` right after Popen through a small `_proc` helper used by the five spawn sites, and call TerminateJobObject in the non-POSIX reap branch. Note that a race remains between Popen returning and the assignment unless the process is created suspended or with PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST. Note also that nested jobs are supported on Windows 8 and later, so an outer CI job does not block this. Or (b) keep the walk and state explicitly that job objects were rejected and why.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that lock_kernel's POSIX leg uses the same primitive git_locking used (flock vs lockf), or justify the change. Cover mixed-version, intra-process and doctor-probe exclusion.
evidence: "take and release both locks through lock_kernel.take_exclusive / release_exclusive"
"Drop the module's own fcntl import"
Root cause: git_locking "imports fcntl itself (:34-37)" — the existing POSIX primitive is not named
"POSIX path unchanged" is stated only for _proc, not for git_locking
findings.finding: Routing git_locking through lock_kernel.take_exclusive changes the POSIX locking primitive too, not just the Windows one. The plan never states that lock_kernel's fcntl leg uses the same call git_locking used before (flock vs fcntl.lockf/F_SETLK). On Linux, flock and POSIX record locks do not exclude each other. Record locks are also per-process: they do not exclude two threads or two fds in one process, and they are dropped when any fd on the file closes. If the primitive differs, three exclusions can silently break: an old-version process versus a new one during upgrade, intra-process serialization of the git-op lock (bug 9305), and the doctor probe of a held lock.
scenarios: Linux/macOS: during a rolling upgrade, an old rebar process holds the git-op lock via flock while a new process takes it via lockf. Both proceed concurrently and the 9305 contention returns.
Single process, two threads each taking the git-op lock: with lockf semantics both acquire, losing serialization that flock previously provided.
Doctor reports the git-op lock as free while it is held, because doctor probes with a different primitive than the holder used.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a failure-disposition line for git_locking's non-contention take/release errors on the new Windows leg: proceed unlocked (advisory) or fatal propagate. Keep release errors from masking a successful op.
evidence: "a platform with neither leg (NoExclusiveLegError) still proceeds unlocked. Same bounded wait, same 'advisory, proceed on exhaustion' contract"
No statement covering non-contention OSError from take_exclusive/release_exclusive on the new Windows leg
findings.finding: The plan states the disposition for only two git_locking failure arms: no lock leg (NoExclusiveLegError, proceed unlocked) and wait exhaustion (advisory, proceed). The new Windows msvcrt leg adds failure modes that never surfaced on Windows before, because the lock used to be a no-op. Examples: OSError/PermissionError opening the lock file, a msvcrt.locking error other than contention, and a release failure. The plan does not say whether these are treated as transient and proceed unlocked, or as fatal and propagate. Before, a Windows caller never saw an exception from these paths.
scenarios: Windows: the store's git common dir is on a read-only or ACL-restricted path, so opening the lock file raises PermissionError. It is unstated whether the git op aborts with a new exception or proceeds unlocked as it did before.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that the _proc descendant walk follows lock_owner._load_kernel32's convention (typed argtypes/restype with wintypes.HANDLE, use_last_error=True + ctypes.get_last_error, an injectable kernel32 for the fake used by test_proc_reap_windows.py), mirrored locally since _proc must stay a dependency-free leaf, or explain why a different seam is needed.
evidence: Plan: "a `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot` walk (ctypes, Windows only) ... each gets `TerminateProcess`"
Plan: "pins the descendant walk ... with a fake snapshot/terminate pair on every platform"
src/rebar/_store/lock_owner.py:261-277 `_load_kernel32()` sets `use_last_error=True`, `OpenProcess.restype = wintypes.HANDLE`, etc., and returns `ctypes.get_last_error`
src/rebar/_store/lock_owner.py:280-292: kernel32/get_last_error are injectable 'so the decision table is testable on any host'
src/rebar/_proc.py:5: 'This stdlib-only leaf remains importable by path-loaded reconciler code' (so importing lock_owner from _proc may not be allowed; mirroring its pattern is the alternative)
findings.finding: The plan adds a new ctypes kernel32 binding to _proc (CreateToolhelp32Snapshot / Process32*W / OpenProcess / TerminateProcess) without mentioning the typed loader the repo already has. src/rebar/_store/lock_owner.py:261-277 (`_load_kernel32`) uses `use_last_error=True`, explicit `argtypes`/`restype` (HANDLE return types), `ctypes.get_last_error`, and an injectable kernel32 for host-independent tests (`_windows_pid_alive(pid, kernel32=..., get_last_error=...)`). The plan's 'fake snapshot/terminate pair' seam and its untyped ctypes calls are a second, different convention for the same job.
scenarios: Without `restype = wintypes.HANDLE`, ctypes' default int return type can truncate the snapshot/process HANDLE on 64-bit Windows. The walk then fails silently into the best-effort debug log, the grandchild survives, and test_harness stays red on Windows.
A future maintainer finds two Windows kernel32 test-seam styles (an injectable kernel32 object vs a fake snapshot/terminate pair) and has to learn both.
findings.suggested_fix: In the _proc bullet, add: "The walk loads kernel32 through a local typed loader that mirrors `lock_owner._load_kernel32` (WinDLL with use_last_error=True; HANDLE/DWORD/BOOL argtypes and restypes for CreateToolhelp32Snapshot, Process32FirstW/NextW, OpenProcess, TerminateProcess, CloseHandle). The kernel32 object is injectable, which is the seam test_proc_reap_windows.py fakes. It is not imported from _store, so _proc stays a stdlib-only leaf."

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a creation-time guard to the Windows descendant walk: a process is a child of P only if its creation time is not earlier than P's. Pin this guard, the stale-parent-pid case, and the reach limit for orphans below depth 1 in test_proc_reap_windows.py.
evidence: "collects processes whose parent-pid chain leads to `proc.pid`, and each gets `TerminateProcess`"
"pins the descendant walk (pure parent-pid closure, deepest-first order, an exited parent's orphan included)"
"the un-waited Popen handle keeps the child's pid from being reused" — true only for proc.pid itself, not for deeper intermediates
findings.finding: The Windows descendant walk is specified as a 'pure parent-pid closure' with no pid-reuse guard. Windows never re-parents, so stale th32ParentProcessID values are common. An unrelated long-running process whose dead parent's pid was later reused by a member of the child's tree would chain to proc.pid and be TerminateProcess'd. The orphan claim also only holds one level below proc.pid: below that level, a dead intermediate's pid is not pinned by any handle.
scenarios: On a Windows runner or dev box, a process started by an exited launcher has a stale parent pid. A tree member reuses that pid, and the reap kills the unrelated process.
A great-grandchild whose grandchild parent exited is missed because the chain breaks at an unpinned, dead pid.
findings.suggested_fix: When building the closure, accept a snapshot entry as a child of pid P only if its creation time (GetProcessTimes via OpenProcess with PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION) is >= P's creation time. For proc.pid, use the creation time of the held Popen handle. Add a fake-snapshot case where a pre-existing process's stale parent pid equals a tree member's pid and assert it is not terminated. Narrow the orphan claim to direct children of proc.pid.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify pid-reuse defences for the walk: parent creation time must precede the child's, and identity is re-checked after OpenProcess before TerminateProcess. Test the reused-ppid case.
evidence: "collects processes whose parent-pid chain leads to proc.pid, and each gets TerminateProcess"
"the un-waited Popen handle keeps the child's pid from being reused" — covers only the direct child
"pins the descendant walk (pure parent-pid closure, deepest-first order, an exited parent's orphan included)"
findings.finding: The descendant walk snapshots the process table and later calls TerminateProcess by pid. The plan guards pid reuse only for the direct child, via the un-waited Popen handle. Intermediate descendants have no open handle. Between the snapshot and OpenProcess/TerminateProcess, a listed pid can exit and be reused by an unrelated process: a check-then-act race. Separately, a pure parent-pid closure can claim an unrelated process whose recorded parent pid was reused by a descendant. The planned unit test pins a 'pure parent-pid closure', which would lock this behaviour in. No creation-time ordering check is specified, i.e. accepting a parent only if it was created before the child, and verifying identity after OpenProcess.
scenarios: Windows: a grandchild exits after the snapshot and its pid is immediately reused by an unrelated user process. The second pass or the terminate loop kills the unrelated process.
Windows: an unrelated process Z's real parent exited and that pid was reused by a descendant of the timed-out child. Z's parent-pid chain now leads to proc.pid and Z is terminated.
findings.suggested_fix: In the walk, accept P as a child of Q only if Q's creation time (GetProcessTimes) precedes P's. After OpenProcess(PROCESS_TERMINATE|PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION), re-read the creation time and skip the process if it differs from the snapshot. Add a fake-snapshot case where a reused parent pid has a later creation time and assert that process is not terminated.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the Windows descendant walk reject PID-reuse false matches: only count a process as a descendant if it was created no earlier than its claimed parent and no earlier than proc (via GetProcessTimes), and pin this with a fake-snapshot case in test_proc_reap_windows.py.
evidence: Plan: "collects processes whose parent-pid chain leads to `proc.pid`, and each gets `TerminateProcess`"

Plan: "the un-waited Popen handle keeps the child's pid from being reused, so the walk also finds a grandchild whose parent already exited" — this guards against reuse after the child is spawned, not against proc.pid or an intermediate pid having been someone else's pid before
src/rebar/_proc.py:32-41: the current Windows path only kills proc itself, so the walk is the first code here that can kill processes rebar did not spawn
Windows recycles PIDs aggressively, and PROCESSENTRY32.th32ParentProcessID is never updated when the parent exits
findings.finding: The Windows descendant walk builds its kill set from the th32ParentProcessID closure alone, so PID reuse can make it TerminateProcess unrelated processes. The plan's safety argument covers only one direction: the un-waited Popen handle stops proc.pid being reused AFTER the child exits. It does not cover proc.pid (or an exited descendant's pid) being a REUSED number. An older, unrelated process whose original parent once had that pid still records it as its parent, so the closure counts it as a descendant and kills it. The plan's headline case, 'an exited parent's orphan included', is exactly where a parent-pid value is stale and this misfire happens.

findings.finding: The descendant walk is a 'pure parent-pid closure' over `th32ParentProcessID`. On Windows the stored parent pid is never updated: it keeps the creator's pid after the creator exits, and that pid can be reused. Before our child was spawned, another process may have had the pid that is now `proc.pid`. Any still-running process created by that earlier owner reports `th32ParentProcessID == proc.pid`, so the closure would call `TerminateProcess` on an unrelated process and on everything below it. The plan's reasoning that 'the un-waited Popen handle keeps the child's pid from being reused' only stops reuse AFTER the child was created. It does not cover older processes whose recorded parent pid already matched before then.
